extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in sociology/criminology, policy analysts and those studying media/policy responses to crime
extracted.subtask_description: Critical, historically-informed analysis of how a particular crime label ('mugging') was constructed, reported, and measured, and how statistics, classification and institutional reactions produced a moral panic. Useful for evaluating media, policing and statistical claims about crime waves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of the crime label / definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the term 'mugging' (or any crime label) is clearly defined. Example given: the Home Secretary's definition — 'robberies by gangs of 2 or more youths on people walking alone in the open' — contained ambiguous terms ('youths', 'in the open') and excluded individual offenders by invoking 'gang'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using or reporting crime figures, require a precise operational definition of the label being counted (who counts as a 'mugger', what circumstances qualify). Note that vague or shifting definitions will distort comparisons and policy responses; examine the original definitions used when figures were compiled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating novelty requires historical comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume a crime is 'new' because a label is new. The text compares the Hills killing to earlier incidents (e.g. the Shaw case) to show the behaviour existed earlier even if not called 'mugging'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show that a phenomenon is genuinely novel, compare it systematically with past cases and patterns rather than relying on the emergence of a new label or recent media attention. Check whether earlier similar incidents were simply categorized differently or ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of crime statistics (six cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime statistics are imperfect indicators for volume of crime because: (1) they refer only to reported crime ('dark figure' excluded); (2) areas collate statistics differently; (3) police sensitisation/targeting increases detections; (4) public anxiety about highlighted offences leads to over-reporting; (5) statistics are based on legal (not sociological) categories and so are arbitrary; (6) changes in the law make strict over-time comparisons difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always evaluate crime statistics with these limitations in mind. Trace sources, check comparability across areas and years, and do not treat headline numbers as objective measures without qualification. Consult methodological reviews (Perks Committee, Cambridge Institute work) and treat reported figures as socially mediated constructs as well as data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution interpreting percentage changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentages (especially percentage differences between two numbers) can be misleading as a 'hard' fact; e.g., headline percentage rises may exaggerate significance without context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require absolute counts, baseline levels, and average annual rates when assessing percent changes. Question dramatic-sounding percentage increases by checking the base rate and time span used to compute them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of statistical provenance (no back-projection without explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some widely cited figures (e.g., 'London muggings up 129% over 4 years') appear to be back-projections or selective conflations and the origin of these reconstructions may be obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand explicit documentation of how reconstructed statistics were produced. If a separate statistical category did not exist in the year being reported, ask how earlier years were re-coded or estimated and whether the method is replicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification / recategorisation effects on trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in subcategories (e.g., 'snatchings', 'thefts from the person', 'robbery and other violent thefts') and the lack of publicly specified differentiation criteria can produce divergent trends and apparent rises or falls that are artifacts of classification shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating trends, check whether category definitions changed over time and whether items migrated between categories. Require the producers of statistics to publish the criteria used to separate subcategories and to show consistent series if they claim trend continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required to claim courts are 'soft' (acquittal vs conviction rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that the courts are 'soft' often rest on assertions about high acquittal rates (e.g., the claim of ~50% acquittals). Empirical studies cited found jury acquittal rates around ~31% and many acquittals resulted from judge-directed acquittals where prosecution evidence was thin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims about courtroom 'softness' by examining reliable studies of acquittal/conviction rates, their denominators (who pleaded not guilty), and the composition of acquittals (minor vs serious cases). Don't accept anecdotal or rounded claims without supporting empirical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess sentencing trends with attention to measurement method
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentencing trends can appear different depending on whether one uses admissions in a year or 'year-end' stock figures. Some analyses (Sparks) show increases in long fixed-term sentences and more lifers, contradicting the notion of lenient sentencing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring sentencing severity, be explicit about metric (admissions, year-end populations, average lengths) and note reforms (e.g., abolition of capital punishment) that affect long-sentence counts. Compare multiple indicators to avoid misleading conclusions based on a single measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing required for deterrence claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption that tougher/ exemplary sentences deter crime must be tested empirically. Home Office research (Baxter and Nuttall) on the Handsworth case found no anticipated impact on reported robberies in the police areas studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To assess deterrence, evaluate local crime time-series before and after sentencing changes, control for policing and reporting changes, and avoid causal inference from coincident trends. Single-case sentencing events are weak evidence of deterrent effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistics as ideological / political instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics and opinion polls can be mobilised to ground impressions in 'hard' numbers and to legitimise policy or punitive responses; the authors quote W. I. Thomas: 'Those things which men believe to be true, are true in their consequences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinise the political uses of statistics: who produced them, for what audience, and what actions they were used to justify. Consider alternative interpretations and be alert to selective presentation that serves an institutional or media narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of time-span must be justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Different time spans yield different impressions (e.g., McClintock & Avison used 1955-65 showing large increases; McDonald using 1948-68 reduced those increases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require justification for the start and end points of any trend analysis. Prefer sensitivity analysis across multiple time spans to show whether conclusions are robust or artifacts of the chosen window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require explicit criteria for new circumstantial categories (e.g., 'violent' thefts)
rubrics_metrics.description: New circumstantial categories (like 'robbery and other violent thefts') were created without stating criteria for what made a theft 'violent', producing confusion about what is being counted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When new categories are introduced, statisticians and agencies should publish the operational criteria used to classify offences. Analysts should not rely on unnamed or implicit criteria when comparing series or making policy recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider media-judiciary-police interplay when evaluating public reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial practices (giving 'exemplary' sentences), editorials, police campaigns (special squads, patrols) and opinion polls together shaped the 'mugging' panic and public demand for tougher action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze institutional interactions (judiciary, press, police, politicians) as part of evaluating a moral panic: who led, who amplified, whose statements set policy direction, and how each actor used statistics and rhetoric to legitimise measures.
